name: Erythromycin (acne)

card.summary: A prescription macrolide antibiotic solution for acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide because acne bacteria can become resistant.
card.note: Often combined with benzoyl peroxide to limit antibiotic resistance.

quick.overview:
Topical erythromycin 2% is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. Reference sources describe it as a mild-to-moderate acne option, typically combined with benzoyl peroxide.

It is a long-established antibiotic, introduced in 1952.
quick.mechanism: It binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis, reducing acne-associated bacteria.
quick.risks: Local dryness, peeling, itching, redness; rare hives. Labels warn of antibiotic-associated colitis. Reference sources note it is usually paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance.

lead: Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic applied to the skin to calm inflamed acne, the red papules and pustules that dominate the look of breakouts. By reducing acne-associated bacteria, it helps lessen active spots and the redness around them, so skin looks clearer and evener over time. It is a macrolide antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis, and a 2% topical solution is labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. [1][2][3]

Dermatology guidance describes topical antibiotics, erythromycin among them, as most often paired with benzoyl peroxide, which limits the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. [1][4][5] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline as part of acne care. [4] Wikipedia notes that resistance to topical macrolides such as erythromycin has risen worldwide with broad antibiotic use. [5]

Preventing breakouts matters for appearance beyond the spots themselves: Wikipedia reports that acne scarring is estimated to affect most people with acne, and that post-inflammatory darkening can persist for months or years in people with darker skin [5]. Erythromycin itself has been on the market since 1952, and its acne uses are topical solutions, gels, pledgets and combination products with benzoyl peroxide [2][3].

A 2026 network meta-analysis of 32 studies (34 randomised trials, 22,645 patients) found topical erythromycin 2% reduced inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesion counts compared with placebo, while its authors cautioned that efficacy was inconsistent across drugs and outcomes and that routine antibiotic monotherapy should be limited [8].

chain: Fewer acne-associated bacteria and less inflammation
Fewer red, inflamed spots and less risk of marks
angle.text: People use topical erythromycin, usually with benzoyl peroxide, to reduce inflamed pimples so skin looks clearer and calmer. Fewer active lesions also means fewer opportunities for lasting marks and scars.

infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia [2]

paras: The US label for erythromycin topical solution 2% lists acne vulgaris as its indication. [3] Grokipedia describes it as used for mild to moderate inflammatory acne, usually combined with benzoyl peroxide. [1] Wikipedia lists erythromycin alongside clindamycin, metronidazole and sulfacetamide as topical antibiotics for mild to moderately severe acne, and says dermatologists prefer to use antibiotics in combination rather than alone. [5]

On T Nation, users discussing hormone-related breakouts have mentioned a prescription routine of benzoyl peroxide wash followed by an erythromycin pad, and another poster listed erythromycin among antibiotics that worked for friends but not for them. [6][7]

sections.h: Combination with benzoyl peroxide and resistance
paras: Wikipedia states that benzoyl peroxide does not appear to cause bacterial resistance, unlike antibiotics, and that pairing the two is common in dermatology [5]. It also reports that broad antibiotic use has raised rates of resistant Cutibacterium acnes worldwide, particularly to tetracyclines and macrolides such as topical erythromycin, and that the Global Alliance to Improve Outcomes in Acne advises against using topical and oral antibiotics together [5].

The 2024 AAD guideline, which used a systematic review and the GRADE approach, includes among its good practice statements combining topical agents with different mechanisms of action and limiting systemic antibiotic use [4]. Wikipedia notes that dermatologists prefer antibiotics as part of combination therapy rather than alone and that oral antibiotic courses are recommended for no longer than three months, with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid added if longer use is needed [5].

The topical label lists occasional local reactions: peeling, dryness, itching, erythema and oiliness, with eye irritation and skin tenderness also reported [3]. Urticarial reactions requiring steroid treatment have been reported [3]. The label carries a warning about pseudomembranous colitis, which has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents [3]. It lists pregnancy category B, noting no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women [3].

Most serious effects described for erythromycin in general reference sources concern the oral form: gastrointestinal upset, QT prolongation, allergic reactions, liver effects and C. difficile colitis; it also inhibits the enzyme CYP3A4, which underlies many oral drug interactions [2]. Wikipedia describes oral erythromycin as appearing safe in pregnancy, apart from the estolate form [2].

Erythromycin is a macrolide that binds the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation, halting protein synthesis; its effect is mainly bacteriostatic [1][2]. Systemically it is also a motilin receptor agonist, which increases gut motility, and this underlies its use for gastroparesis; that action is unrelated to its acne use [2].

Erythromycin was launched as Ilosone by Eli Lilly in 1952, named after Iloilo province in the Philippines, and Lilly was granted a patent in 1953 [2]. Wikipedia credits the Filipino scientist Abelardo Aguilar with isolating it from a soil-derived strain and sending samples to Lilly, and states that he received no credit or compensation [2]. Clarithromycin was later developed to overcome erythromycin's instability in stomach acid, and Woodward's total synthesis of erythromycin was published in 1981 [2]. Topical erythromycin solutions were later developed for acne, and today the drug is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia [2][3].

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline, a systematic review with graded recommendations, strongly recommends topical antibiotics for acne, alongside benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and oral doxycycline [4].

A 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis in Clinical Drug Investigation pooled randomised trials comparing topical antibiotic monotherapy with placebo or other topical antibiotics (32 studies, 34 trials, 22,645 patients). Against placebo, dapsone 5% and erythromycin 2% significantly reduced inflammatory lesions, and azithromycin 2%, erythromycin 2%, metronidazole 2% and minocycline 4% reduced non-inflammatory lesions; no treatment significantly improved total lesion counts, and only clindamycin 1% and minocycline 4% formulations could be shown superior on investigator global assessment success because of inconsistent reporting. The authors concluded that efficacy was inconsistent and safety uncertain, and that routine antibiotic monotherapy should be limited [8].
Other trials of erythromycin in the literature concern non-acne conditions such as gastrointestinal and obstetric uses.

timeline.event: Erythromycin launched as Ilosone by Eli Lilly. [2]
Woodward's total synthesis of erythromycin published. [2]
AAD acne guideline strongly recommends topical antibiotics alongside benzoyl peroxide, retinoids and oral doxycycline. [4]
Network meta-analysis of topical antibiotic trials reports lesion reductions for erythromycin 2% and cautions against routine monotherapy. [8]

lore.intro: Erythromycin for acne appears mostly in passing in T Nation threads about breakouts, hormone therapy and whether to use isotretinoin [6][7]. The recurring theme is antibiotics as an alternative or a first step before stronger options.

claims.claim: An erythromycin pad plus a benzoyl peroxide wash is a prescription routine for stubborn breakouts.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster suggested getting a benzoyl peroxide wash prescribed and following it with an erythromycin pad. [6]
claims.experts: Guidelines describe topical antibiotics combined with benzoyl peroxide as a recommended approach. [4][5]

claims.claim: Antibiotics work for some people and not others.
claims.believers: A poster listed erythromycin among antibiotics that worked for friends but not for them. [7]
claims.experts: The 2026 meta-analysis found inconsistent efficacy across lesion types for topical antibiotics. [8]

claims.claim: A topical antibiotic alone is enough to clear acne.
claims.believers: Forum mentions treat an antibiotic as a stand-alone step before considering isotretinoin. [7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says dermatologists prefer antibiotics in combination rather than alone, and the 2026 meta-analysis said routine monotherapy should be limited. [5][8]

claims.claim: Using antibiotics for acne carries no downside beyond skin irritation.
claims.believers: Forum mentions focus on whether the pad worked rather than on resistance. [6][7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports rising resistance to topical macrolides worldwide, and the label warns of colitis. [3][5]
